---
title: "Get started"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  dev = "ragg_png",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.4,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

bauhaus turns a ggplot into one of the sixteen day dials of the Bauhaus Clock screensaver. Each
theme lays the plot on the dial's paper plate with the screensaver's fine grain, sets type in the
screensaver's typeface, and colours text, grid lines, geoms and scales with the inks measured from
that dial.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(bauhaus)
```

## A first plot

Build a plot as usual and add `theme_bauhaus()`. The default dial is Turquoise, the screensaver's
own default.

```{r first}
penguins <- na.omit(palmerpenguins::penguins)

p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, alpha = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Palmer penguins",
    subtitle = "Body mass against flipper length",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species",
    caption = "Data: palmerpenguins"
  )

p + theme_bauhaus()
```

Pick another dial by name. Case, spaces and underscores don't matter, so `"Signal Blue"`,
`"signal-blue"` and `"signal_blue"` are the same dial.

```{r dials}
bauhaus_dial_names(display = TRUE)
```

```{r ocean}
p + theme_bauhaus("ocean")
```

Each dial also has a shortcut: `theme_bauhaus_ocean()`, `theme_bauhaus_signal_blue()` and so on.

```{r yellow}
p + theme_bauhaus_yellow()
```

## What a theme sets

A Bauhaus theme is a complete ggplot2 theme. It sets:

| Part | Taken from the dial |
|---|---|
| Plot background | The plate, lifted by 13/255 as the screensaver lifts it, with the paper grain at the strength measured for that dial. White has no grain; Tennis has the most. |
| Type | Zalando Sans Expanded, the screensaver's typeface. Titles and strip labels use the semibold weight. |
| Titles, axis titles, default geom colour | The hour-numeral ink. |
| Subtitle, caption, axis labels, ticks, grid | The minute-track ink. Ticks and grid lines have round ends, like the track's ticks. On Cream and Slate, whose track ink is very faint, the colour is pushed towards the numeral ink until it reads clearly. |
| Discrete colour and fill | The dial's eight-colour palette. |
| Continuous colour and fill | The dial's sequential palette. |
| Accent (e.g. `geom_smooth()`) | The second colour of the discrete palette. |

So the theme alone gives you matching colours. Here is the same chart with discrete and continuous
fills:

```{r palettes-auto, fig.height = 4}
bars <- ggplot(mpg, aes(class, fill = drv)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Cars by class", x = NULL, y = "Count", fill = "Drive")

bars + theme_bauhaus("salmon", grid = "x")
```

```{r continuous, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(faithfuld, aes(waiting, eruptions, fill = density)) +
  geom_raster() +
  coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Old Faithful", x = "Waiting time (min)", y = "Eruption (min)", fill = "Density") +
  theme_bauhaus("glacier")
```

Single-colour geoms use the numeral ink, and smoothers use the accent:

```{r single}
ggplot(economics, aes(date, unemploy / 1000)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, span = 0.3) +
  labs(title = "US unemployment", x = NULL, y = "Unemployed (millions)") +
  theme_bauhaus("rose")
```

## Options

`theme_bauhaus()` takes the usual `base_size`, `base_family` and `header_family`, plus a few of its
own:

* `grid`: which major grid lines to draw, `"xy"` (the default), `"x"`, `"y"` or `"none"`.
* `grain`: `TRUE` for the dial's measured grain, `FALSE` for a flat plate, or a number to set the
  strength (standard deviation in 8-bit code values).
* `grain_density`: grain samples per inch. The default, 150, matches the screensaver on a Retina
  laptop screen; lower it for a coarser grain.

```{r options}
p + theme_bauhaus("beige", base_size = 12, grid = "y", grain = 9, grain_density = 90)
```

To use a dial for every plot in a session, set it once:

```{r theme-set, eval = FALSE}
theme_set(theme_bauhaus("pistachio"))
```

## Scales

The theme already sets each dial's palettes as the defaults. Add a scale when you want another
dial's palette, a reversed one, or other scale arguments.

```{r scales, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy, colour = cty)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_bauhaus_b("tennis", n.breaks = 6) +
  labs(title = "Binned colour scale", x = "Displacement (l)", y = "Highway mpg", colour = "City mpg") +
  theme_bauhaus("tennis")
```

| Scale | Data | Palette |
|---|---|---|
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_d()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_d()` | discrete | eight colours |
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_c()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_c()` | continuous | sequential ramp |
| `scale_colour_bauhaus_b()`, `scale_fill_bauhaus_b()` | binned | sequential ramp in steps |

The palettes are also available as plain colour vectors and palette functions, for base graphics or
other packages:

```{r palette-vectors}
bauhaus_palette("turquoise")
bauhaus_palette("turquoise", type = "sequential", n = 5)
pal_bauhaus("noir")(3)
```

See the [palettes article](palettes.html) for every dial's colours.

## The raw colours

`bauhaus_colours()` returns everything measured for a dial, which is handy for annotations:

```{r colours}
col <- bauhaus_colours("lavender")
col
```

```{r annotate}
ggplot(economics, aes(date, psavert)) +
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = as.Date("2007-12-01"), xmax = as.Date("2009-06-01"), ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = col[["shadow_ambient"]], alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  annotate("text",
    x = as.Date("2007-09-01"), y = 15, label = "Great Recession", hjust = 1,
    colour = col[["track"]], family = bauhaus_font_family(), size = 3.5
  ) +
  labs(title = "Personal saving rate", x = NULL, y = "% of disposable income") +
  theme_bauhaus("lavender")
```

## Fonts and graphics devices

The package bundles Zalando Sans Expanded (SIL Open Font License) and registers it with
**systemfonts** when it loads, so nothing needs installing. Devices built on systemfonts find it
automatically:

* **ragg**: `ggsave()` uses it for PNG, JPEG and TIFF whenever ragg is installed. In R Markdown and
  Quarto, set the chunk option `dev = "ragg_png"`. In RStudio, choose *Tools › Global Options ›
  General › Graphics › Backend: AGG*. Positron uses ragg when it is installed.
* **svglite** for SVG.

Other devices don't know the bundled font. `pdf()` and `postscript()` fall back to Helvetica, and
the default Windows and macOS screen devices to their system sans. To get the real typeface there,
render text with showtext:

```{r showtext, eval = FALSE}
bauhaus_showtext() # registers the fonts with showtext and turns it on
pdf("plot.pdf", width = 7, height = 4.5)
print(p + theme_bauhaus())
dev.off()
```

Or use the Cairo PDF device, `ggsave("plot.pdf", device = cairo_pdf)`, after installing the font
files from `bauhaus_font_files()` on your system.

## Saving

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
ggsave("penguins.png", p + theme_bauhaus("ocean"), width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 300)
```

`ggsave()` takes the background colour from the theme. The grain is drawn as a raster image, which
works on every device but makes PDF and SVG files larger. For vector output you can switch it off
for the whole session:

```{r grain-off, eval = FALSE}
options(bauhaus.grain = FALSE)
```

## Combining plots with patchwork

Each plot draws its own grained background. When you combine plots with
[patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com), give the whole layout the theme too, so the
space around and between the plots is paper as well:

```{r patchwork, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
library(patchwork)

a <- ggplot(penguins, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")
b <- ggplot(penguins, aes(species, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count")

(a | b) +
  plot_annotation(title = "Penguins", theme = theme_bauhaus("sky_blue")) &
  theme_bauhaus("sky_blue")
```
